Behind her, a richly painted background with layered painterly colour, subtle visible brushwork, atmospheric perspective and cinematic depth. Her element — molybdenum: a hard silver-grey metal whose name comes from the Greek word for lead, because the soft, greasy black mineral molybdenite, which leaves a silvery streak on paper, was long confused with graphite and with lead ore; in 1778 it was boiled in nitric acid into a white earth that was neither, and in 1781 freed as metal; it melts above 2600 degrees Celsius, and a little of it keeps steel strong and unbending when hot, in bicycle frames, aircraft, turbines and gun barrels; one atom of it sits at the heart of the enzyme that pulls nitrogen from the air in the root nodules of beans and peas — may show in the outfit's details, motifs or small accessories.
